title: Structure of Atom
short_intro: The structure of the atom encompasses the nuclear model surrounded by orbiting electrons governed by quantum mechanics. It forms the foundation for understanding atomic spectra, electron configurations, and multi-electron coupling phenomena.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Bohr's model of hydrogen atom, radii and velocities of orbits, energy levels, excitation, ionization, and hydrogen spectrum series (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen, Brackett, Pfund).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Spatial quantization, electron spin, Pauli's exclusion principle, L-S coupling (Russell-Saunders coupling), j-j coupling, and vector atom model.

prerequisites: Rutherford alpha-scattering experiment and impact parameter
Planck's quantum theory and de Broglie wavelength
Basic vector algebra and quantum numbers

concept_notes.heading: Bohr's Postulates and Quantization of Angular Momentum
bullets: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain stable, non-radiating circular orbits called stationary states.
The angular momentum of an orbiting electron is quantized as an integral multiple of h/2π.
Radiation is emitted or absorbed only when an electron transitions between two allowed energy states according to hν = E_2 - E_1.

concept_notes.heading: Spatial Quantization and Electron Spin
bullets: Spatial quantization refers to the restriction of the orientation of angular momentum vectors in space relative to an external magnetic field.
Electron spin is an intrinsic angular momentum characterized by spin quantum number s = 1/2 and magnetic spin quantum number m_s = ±1/2.
The total angular momentum vector and its z-component are quantized, giving rise to space quantization.

concept_notes.heading: Pauli's Exclusion Principle and Electronic Configuration
bullets: No two electrons in an atom can have the exact same set of all four quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s).
Each orbital can accommodate a maximum of two electrons with opposite spins.
This principle explains the periodic table structure and shell capacities given by 2n^2.

concept_notes.heading: Coupling Schemes (L-S and j-j Coupling)
bullets: In L-S (Russell-Saunders) coupling, individual orbital angular momenta (l_i) couple to form total L, and spin angular momenta (s_i) couple to form total S; L and S then couple to form total J.
L-S coupling is valid for light and medium-weight atoms where spin-orbit interaction is weaker than electrostatic repulsion.
In j-j coupling, individual orbital and spin angular momenta couple first for each electron (j_i = l_i + s_i), and then these j_i vectors couple to form the total angular momentum J.

derivations.title: Radius and Velocity of n-th Bohr Orbit
derivations.conditions: Circular orbit of an electron around a stationary nucleus of atomic number Z
steps: Equate electrostatic force to centripetal force: \frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \frac{Ze^2}{r^2} = \frac{mv^2}{r}
Apply Bohr's quantization condition for angular momentum: mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}
Eliminate velocity v from the two equations to solve for radius r_n
Substitute r_n back into the velocity equation to get v_n
derivations.result: r_n = \frac{\epsilon_0 n^2 h^2}{\pi m Z e^2} and v_n = \frac{Ze^2}{2 \epsilon_0 n h}

derivations.title: Total Energy of Electron in n-th Bohr Orbit
steps: Sum kinetic and potential energy: E = K + U = -\frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0} \frac{Ze^2}{2r}
Substitute the expression for r_n into the total energy equation
derivations.result: E_n = -\frac{m Z^2 e^4}{8 \epsilon_0^2 h^2 n^2} = -13.6 \frac{Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Level Diagram of Hydrogen Atom
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Horizontal energy lines plotted against vertical energy scale in eV, showing converging levels towards 0 eV and spectral series transitions.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates discrete energy states, ionization energy at 13.6 eV, and different series (Lyman in UV, Balmer in visible, Paschen/Brackett in IR).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on minimum/maximum wavelength of spectral series and excitation energy calculations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Frank-Hertz Experiment Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Collector current versus accelerating potential graph showing periodic drops corresponding to excitation potentials.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves the existence of discrete atomic energy levels as postulated by Bohr.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions on mercury vapor excitation potential (4.9 eV) and inelastic collisions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stern-Gerlach Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Splitting of a beam of silver atoms passing through an inhomogeneous magnetic field into two distinct traces.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates space quantization and spatial orientation of intrinsic electron spin angular momentum (m_s = ±1/2).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on space quantization and spin degrees of freedom.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series in the hydrogen spectrum. (Given R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1)
solution_steps: Identify the transitions for the first line of Balmer series: n_1 = 2 and n_2 = 3.

solved_numericals.question: Find the possible values of total angular momentum quantum number J for two electrons with orbital quantum numbers l_1 = 1 and l_2 = 1 under L-S coupling.
solution_steps: For l_1 = 1 and l_2 = 1, total orbital angular momentum L can take values from |l_1 - l_2| to l_1 + l_2, i.e., L = 0, 1, 2.
For two electrons, individual spins are s_1 = 1/2 and s_2 = 1/2. Total spin S can take values 0 and 1.
Total angular momentum J for each (L, S) combination ranges from |L - S| to L + S.
solved_numericals.answer: J values are 0, 1, 2, and 3 depending on the L and S state combinations.

solved_numericals.question: What is the radius of the third orbit of a hydrogen atom? (Bohr radius r_1 = 0.53 Å)
solution_steps: Use the radius relation for hydrogen-like atoms: r_n = r_1 \times (n^2 / Z).
For hydrogen, Z = 1, and for the third orbit, n = 3.

assumptions_and_limitations: Bohr's model assumes circular orbits, whereas Sommerfeld later introduced elliptical orbits with relativistic corrections.
Bohr's theory is strictly applicable only to single-electron systems (hydrogen, He^+, Li^2+) and fails for multi-electron atoms due to inter-electronic repulsions.
Bohr's model treats electrons as classical particles with precise trajectories, violating Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Bohr's orbits are three-dimensional spherical shells.
common_misconceptions.correct: Bohr's stationary states are planar circular orbits, whereas quantum mechanical orbitals are three-dimensional probability distribution regions.
common_misconceptions.why: Bohr's model is semi-classical and predates wave mechanics and the Schrödinger equation.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Total energy of an orbiting electron is positive.
common_misconceptions.correct: The total energy of a bound electron in an atom is negative.
common_misconceptions.why: Negative energy signifies a bound state where external work is required to remove the electron to infinity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: L-S coupling applies strictly to all heavy atoms.
common_misconceptions.correct: L-S coupling is valid mainly for light atoms, whereas j-j coupling is preferred for heavy atoms where spin-orbit interaction is dominant.
common_misconceptions.why: Electrostatic forces dominate in light atoms, while relativistic spin-orbit interactions dominate in heavy nuclear fields.

quick_revision: Radius of n-th orbit is proportional to n^2/Z, and velocity is proportional to Z/n.
Total energy of hydrogen in state n is E_n = -13.6/n^2 eV.
Lyman series lies in ultraviolet, Balmer in visible, and Paschen/Brackett/Pfund in infrared regions.
Pauli's exclusion principle states no two electrons can share all four quantum numbers (n, l, m_l, m_s).
In L-S coupling, L and S couple to form J; in j-j coupling, individual j_i vector components couple to form total J.
